title: Set Intersection Size At Least Two
statement: Each entry `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]` stands for every integer from `start_i` up to `end_i`, both ends included. Choose a set of integers so that every interval holds at least two of the chosen integers. Return the smallest number of integers such a set can have.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every subset of points is exponential. Instead, handle the intervals by their right end, smallest first. When an interval still lacks points, it should get points as far to the right as possible: they serve it just as well, and every interval handled later ends at or after this one, so right-hand points are the ones most likely to lie inside those later intervals too. Because each new point is placed at the current right end, the chosen points only grow, and only the two largest can still matter.

## Approach

1. Sort by `end` ascending; for equal ends put the larger `start` (the narrower interval) first.
2. Keep `count` and the two largest chosen points, `secondLargest < largest`, both `-1` at first.
3. If `start > largest`, the interval holds no chosen point: add `end - 1` and `end` and count 2.
4. Otherwise, if `start > secondLargest`, it holds only `largest`: add `end`, shift `largest` into `secondLargest`, and count 1.
5. Otherwise it already holds two chosen points. Return `count` at the end.

## Example 1, step by step

`intervals = [[1,3],[3,7],[8,9]]` is already sorted. `[1,3]`: `1 > -1`, so pick 2 and 3 (`count = 2`, points `2, 3`). `[3,7]`: 3 is not above `largest = 3` but is above `secondLargest = 2`, so only 3 is inside; pick 7 (`count = 3`, points `3, 7`). `[8,9]`: `8 > 7`, pick 8 and 9 (`count = 5`). The answer is `5`, from the set `{2, 3, 7, 8, 9}`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the sort; the scan is O(n).
- Space: O(1) besides the sort.

## Pitfalls

- Ties on `end` must put the larger `start` first. Otherwise, on `[[0,2],[2,5],[4,5],[5,7]]`, `[2,5]` picks 5, then `[4,5]` picks 5 again and the count goes wrong (4 instead of 5).
- Compare with strict `>`: a point equal to `start` is inside the interval.
- Only counts are returned, but the points must stay the real largest two; update `secondLargest` before `largest`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | number of points chosen so far |
| `largest` | the largest chosen point |
| `secondLargest` | the second largest chosen point |
| `start`, `end` | ends of the current interval |

narration.2: Sort by right end; for equal ends, the interval with the larger start (the narrower one) comes first.
narration.3: No points have been chosen yet.
narration.4: The two largest chosen points start below every possible value, as no point exists yet.
narration.7: Handle the intervals in order of their right end.
narration.8: Even the largest chosen point is left of this interval, so it holds none of them.
narration.10: Pick the two rightmost integers, end - 1 and end, so later intervals can reuse them.
narration.12: Only the largest chosen point is inside; the interval needs one more.
narration.14: The old largest point becomes the second largest...
narration.15: ...and the new point, placed at end, becomes the largest.
narration.18: Every interval now holds two chosen points; return how many were used.
